sections.heading: 1605, 1606 and the making of an anniversary
paragraphs: The Plot and its commemoration belong to different stages of the history. The conspirators intended to attack the opening of Parliament on 5 November 1605. After the discovery, Parliament met in January 1606 and established an annual thanksgiving. Services and sermons therefore helped reproduce an official account of deliverance long before the Victorian period examined in this collection. The date became a recurring occasion on which political and religious loyalties were publicly expressed.

The statutory observance remained in force until 1859. Its repeal is a useful dividing point within the nineteenth-century material, but it does not imply that local festivities immediately stopped. Legal obligation, church observance, street entertainment and family custom followed different timetables. The chronology makes it possible to place a particular source on the appropriate side of this change.

sections.heading: Historical romance and the Victorian view of 1605
paragraphs: Ainsworth’s Guy Fawkes identifies itself as an historical romance. Its dedication is dated 26 July 1841, placing its treatment of the conspiracy firmly within Victorian publishing. A historical novel can use recognisable names, locations and political events while inventing conversations, motives and private encounters. The four chapters included here should consequently be read as evidence of nineteenth-century storytelling about the Plot, alongside the separate historical account.

This distinction also matters when reading a remembered childhood scene, a folklore collection or a newspaper survey. A reminiscence looks back from a later date; a collector selects and classifies customs; a reporter describes events for a particular readership. Because each was written for a different purpose, the anthology prints several kinds of writing side by side.

sections.heading: Hardy’s Egdon Heath and the scale of the custom
paragraphs: The Return of the Native opens its human action among Fifth of November fires on Egdon Heath. In the novel, neighbouring fires can be seen across the dark landscape, people gather and talk beside them, and a separate fire becomes a signal between Eustacia Vye and Wildeve. Hardy thus gives the observance both a communal setting and a particular place within the plot.

The Egdon material offers a concrete comparison with the regional customs elsewhere in the collection. Notice who collects fuel, who gathers, what the fire makes visible and what conversation takes place around it. The edition’s separate treatment of food, manufacture and policing then supplies other records against which a fictional gathering can be considered.

sections.heading: A card with an identifiable maker and date
paragraphs: One unusually well-documented object is the Christmas card commissioned by Henry Cole and designed by John Callcott Horsley in 1843. Cole’s diary records receiving Horsley’s design on 17 December. The card combines a central family toast with smaller scenes of charitable giving. It joins two subjects that recur throughout Victorian Christmas writing: celebration within the household and responsibility towards people outside it.

A thousand copies were printed, with space for a personal greeting, and the design was offered for sale at a shilling. The V&A’s account records that the venture initially failed commercially. So the surviving card records one experiment in Christmas printing; it does not show that everyone took up the custom straight away. Price, production and the later expansion of the market remain part of its history.

sections.heading: The royal tree before and after 1848
paragraphs: The Royal Collection’s account traces royal Christmas trees to Queen Charlotte before Victoria’s reign. Albert helped popularise a practice that already had a history in Britain. This earlier evidence matters because an account beginning only with Victoria and Albert can mistake the spread of a custom for its first appearance.

The familiar illustration of the royal family around a decorated tree appeared in the Illustrated London News in 1848. It gave readers a reproducible image of a royal domestic celebration. Trees, presents and the grouping of adults and children could then be encountered on the printed page as well as in an actual household. The relationship between private observance and public illustration is a useful subject when reading the book’s chapters on publishing and material culture.

sections.heading: Dickens in a weekly journal
paragraphs: A Christmas Tree appeared in Household Words on 21 December 1850, in issue 39 of the journal’s second volume. This is a different publication setting from the separate gift-book format of A Christmas Carol in 1843. The dated journal record allows the piece to be placed within the seasonal publishing trade discussed in this cultural history.

The three complete Dickens pieces reproduced in the Astor volume give readers primary literary texts alongside the historical chapters. When following one custom through the book, keep the kind of evidence in view: a surviving card shows a manufactured object; an illustration shows a published representation; a literary piece shows a writer arranging material for readers. Comparing these forms makes it possible to ask precise questions about what Christmas looked like, who could afford its goods and how its familiar images circulated.

sections.heading: Performance before publication
paragraphs: The first surviving performance record places Othello at the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 1 November 1604, performed by the King’s Men. That record establishes that the play existed by this date; it does not identify the first occasion on which it was ever acted. The gap between performance and the first printing in 1622 is nearly eighteen years.

The 1622 quarto title page advertises performances at both the Globe and Blackfriars. Thomas Walkley entered the play in the Stationers’ Register in 1621 and published the quarto the following year. These details belong to the history of the surviving book: they show how the play was presented for sale after a substantial theatrical life.

sections.heading: Differences a reader can locate
paragraphs: The Folio version is about 160 lines longer than the first quarto. Its differences include extended passages as well as individual words. One well-known example occurs in Othello’s account of his courtship: the quarto has Desdemona respond with a world of sighs, while the Folio gives a world of kisses. The alternatives describe different behaviour and cannot both occupy the same place in a reading text.

The early editions also contain different forms of oaths and interjections. Some omissions have been associated with theatrical censorship, but the origin of every difference cannot be securely reconstructed. Comparison therefore begins with what the printed witnesses actually contain. Explanations based on revision, stage practice or copying are arguments to be weighed; the later date of publication does not prove them.

sections.heading: The handkerchief as a sequence of stage actions
paragraphs: The handkerchief’s route can be followed scene by scene. Desdemona drops it while trying to attend to Othello; Emilia retrieves it and passes it to Iago. Cassio subsequently finds it in his lodging and asks Bianca to copy the embroidery. When Bianca returns it, Othello observes an exchange whose background he has not witnessed.

This sequence is useful for reading the commentary because the audience’s information differs from Othello’s at each stage. The same distinction applies when Iago questions Cassio about Bianca while allowing Othello to believe the subject is Desdemona. Recording who is present, who can hear and what each person already knows provides a precise basis for analysing a performance. It also prevents Iago’s account of an event from being confused with the action shown onstage.

sections.heading: An eyewitness at the Globe
paragraphs: Simon Forman’s Book of Plays preserves an account of seeing Macbeth at the Globe on 20 April, normally dated 1611. His manuscript gives 1610, but the date is corrected in the Shakespeare Documented catalogue. It is an eyewitness record of a performance, not a transcript of the play. Forman records the principal actions and the lessons he took from them.

The distinction is useful when setting his account beside the Folio printed twelve years later. An audience member may omit a scene, misunderstand a detail or concentrate on a particular moral. The record establishes a performance and preserves what one spectator noticed; it cannot by itself recover every speech or prove that a passage absent from his summary was absent from the stage.

sections.heading: Holinshed and the treatment of Banquo
paragraphs: Shakespeare drew on the Scottish history in the 1587 edition of Holinshed’s Chronicles. One substantial alteration concerns Banquo: in the chronicle narrative he assists Macbeth’s conspiracy against Duncan, whereas Shakespeare’s Banquo does not take part in the murder. His knowledge of the witches’ predictions nevertheless makes him dangerous to the new king.

James VI of Scotland, who became James I of England in 1603, traced his ancestry to Banquo. That claim forms part of the play’s early Stuart context and helps explain why scholars attend closely to the procession of future kings. The historical connection can be documented while particular claims about Shakespeare’s intentions require a separate argument from the play and its circumstances.

sections.heading: What survives in the Folio
paragraphs: The 1623 Folio is the only early printed authority for Macbeth, so an editor cannot compare an earlier quarto against it as in Hamlet or Othello. The Hecate passages and song references have attracted particular attention because of their relationship to material in Thomas Middleton’s The Witch. The extent and timing of any adaptation remain questions within the textual history.

Other performance decisions arise directly from the dramatic action. A bell signals Macbeth to go to Duncan’s chamber; knocking interrupts the aftermath; the banquet requires Macbeth to respond to Banquo’s ghost while the guests respond to Macbeth. Later, a doctor and gentlewoman watch Lady Macbeth walking in her sleep. Reading these scenes through their entrances, sounds, objects and witnesses distinguishes the words preserved by the text from choices a production must make about visibility, timing and movement.

sections.heading: More than one state of the first printing
paragraphs: The 1608 quarto presents problems within the printing itself. Corrections were made while the sheets were being produced, so surviving copies can preserve different readings on what appears to be the same page. Verse is sometimes printed as prose, and some prose is divided into verse lines. Comparison therefore involves the state of a particular copy as well as the broad distinction between quarto and Folio.

A second quarto was printed in 1619 but retained a 1608 date on its title page. It largely reprints the first quarto, introducing corrections and further errors. The false date was identified by later bibliographical research. References to Q1 and Q2 consequently distinguish two printings that cannot be dated reliably from their title pages alone.

sections.heading: A version-specific scene and the older sources
paragraphs: The Folio omits the whole scene commonly numbered 4.3 in conflated editions. In that scene, a Gentleman reports Cordelia’s response to news of her father. Its inclusion gives the reader an account of her feelings before Lear and Cordelia meet again. The passage is a concrete example of why a conflated text has a different sequence of information from either early version read separately.

Shakespeare also changed the inherited story. Holinshed’s account, drawing on Geoffrey of Monmouth, allows the youngest daughter to help restore her father to power. The separate Gloucester plot draws on a story in Sidney’s Arcadia involving a father deceived and blinded through the actions of an illegitimate son. These sources help identify what Shakespeare combined, retained and altered; they do not make the resulting tragedy a report of historical events.

sections.heading: Dover and the evidence available onstage
paragraphs: Gloucester asks Edgar to guide him to the edge of a cliff. Edgar describes a great height while keeping his father on level ground, then changes his voice and pretends to encounter a man who has survived a fall. The audience can watch the discrepancy between Gloucester’s belief and the action being performed.

This scene offers a practical way to use the edition’s attention to blindness, language and performance. Establish what the stage shows, what Edgar describes and what Gloucester can perceive. Then follow the changes in Edgar’s assumed identity and his explanation of the supposed rescue. The passage’s effects depend on how speech supplies a landscape that the actors do not physically occupy, and on the different knowledge held by father, son and audience.

sections.heading: The 1600 quarto and the later false date
paragraphs: Thomas Fisher registered A Midsummer Night’s Dream on 8 October 1600. The first quarto was printed that year by Richard Braddock for Fisher. It is the earliest printed witness and the principal basis identified for this Astor edition. Its date should be distinguished from the probable date of composition in the middle of the 1590s.

The second quarto also bears a 1600 date, but bibliographical research assigns its printing to 1619. It was prepared from the first quarto with some alterations, and an annotated copy of that reprint subsequently supplied copy for the 1623 Folio. The three texts therefore form a history of reprinting and intervention; they are not three independent surviving manuscripts by Shakespeare.

sections.heading: A change in the cast of the final act
paragraphs: The Folio’s substitution of Egeus for Philostrate in Act 5 changes which character discusses the available entertainments with Theseus. Egeus is Hermia’s father, whose demand concerning her marriage begins the play’s central conflict. Philostrate is the official responsible for arranging the court’s festivities. Their dramatic functions are different even when substantially the same lines are assigned to them.

The Astor edition retains Philostrate, as stated in its textual description. The variant remains useful for readers and performers because it shows that a speech heading can carry as much dramatic consequence as a changed word within a speech. Deciding who remains present at a wedding celebration also changes the visible group receiving the mechanicals’ performance.

sections.heading: The mechanicals make a play
paragraphs: The preparation of Pyramus and Thisbe records several practical stages of amateur production: allocating parts, arranging a rehearsal, deciding how to represent the wall and moonlight, and worrying about the effect of a lion on the audience. Quince directs a company whose members continue to explain their devices even while performing them.

At court, the spectators interrupt and comment on the entertainment, while the players attempt to continue. The scene therefore supplies a precise vocabulary for discussing the play’s interest in theatrical representation: actor and part, object and imagined setting, spoken explanation and visible action. Read the rehearsal beside the final performance to see which problems the company anticipated, which solutions it adopted and how the court receives them. The contrast is available in the scene sequence itself, without requiring a claim that the mechanicals represent a single identifiable real company.

sections.heading: Dating the three printed witnesses
paragraphs: The First Quarto appeared in 1603. It is much shorter than the later versions and includes different character names: Polonius appears as Corambis and Reynaldo as Montano. It also arranges some material differently. Describing it simply as an abridgement misses differences in wording and dramatic sequence whose origins remain disputed.

The Second Quarto survives with title pages dated 1604 and 1605. It was printed by James Roberts for Nicholas Ling and advertised its enlarged text as based on a true and perfect copy. That wording is the publisher’s claim on the title page. The Folio of 1623 supplies another text, with both omissions and additions in relation to Q2, as well as hundreds of smaller differences.

sections.heading: What a conflated reading text can contain
paragraphs: Conflation brings material from more than one early witness into a continuous edition, but it cannot print mutually exclusive readings in the same position. An editor still has to choose between alternative words and decide how to place passages absent from one version. The result should not be mistaken for a surviving manuscript in that combined form.

This distinction is particularly relevant to the Astor volume’s stated Q2 basis and inclusion of important Folio material. Start with one line or passage, note which early text has it, then read the other version and see what changes. Claims about Shakespearean revision, theatrical cutting or imperfect transmission require evidence beyond the mere existence of a difference.

sections.heading: The court’s papers and the play’s documents
paragraphs: Writing has a practical role throughout Hamlet. Polonius reads Hamlet’s letter to Ophelia before the king and queen. Hamlet writes in his tables after the Ghost’s departure. Later he obtains the commission carrying Claudius’s instructions to England and substitutes another, using his father’s signet to seal it. Letters delivered to Horatio report the interruption of the voyage and Hamlet’s return.

These documents differ in authorship, audience and control. The love letter becomes evidence when removed from its original exchange; the commission carries an order meant to be obeyed abroad; Hamlet’s replacement depends on the authority of a seal. Following who writes, carries, opens and reads each document offers a concrete route through the play’s treatment of knowledge and power. The account of the voyage is itself delivered retrospectively, so the reader should distinguish the actions Hamlet reports from events presented directly before the theatre audience.
